title: Works of the Law
lead: The Greek phrase erga nomou, 'works of the law', is used by Paul in Romans and Galatians for what is not the basis on which a person is justified (Galatians 2:16; 3:2, 5, 10; Romans 3:20, 28). Whether it means all the deeds the law requires, or the practices that marked Jews off from other peoples (circumcision, Sabbath, food laws), is one of the main disputes about Paul. The Hebrew phrase ma'ase ha-torah appears in the Dead Sea text 4QMMT.

sections.b: The traditional Protestant reading, from Luther and Calvin, takes the phrase to mean every deed the law commands, which no one can fully keep. The New Perspective (Dunn, Wright) takes it to mean especially the practices that marked Jews as God's people. Others (Moo, Schreiner) reply that Paul speaks of the whole law and its demands, and that Jewish identity is the way the law worked. Catholic readers have usually taken the phrase to mean the ritual law of Moses and have kept room for good works done in grace.
